title: Comfort, Trouble and a Changed Plan
sum: Paul writes to the church in Corinth, and to the believers around it, after a hard stretch in his own life and in the church's. He opens with a prayer of blessing to the God of all comfort (1:3–7), and the word "comfort" and its relatives come ten times in five verses. The comfort he has received in his troubles, he says, overflows to others, as the sufferings of Christ overflow toward him. Then he tells the Corinthians how, in the province of Asia, he came so near to death that he gave up hope of living (1:8–11).

The second half (1:12–24) turns to a charge against him. He had promised to visit and had not come, and some in Corinth said he was unreliable, a man who says "Yes" and "No" at once. Paul answers that his word rests on God's faithfulness, because every promise of God is "Yes" in Christ, that God himself has set his seal on Paul and the church together, and that he stayed away to spare them. The chapter introduces the letter's two great themes: strength through weakness, and the integrity of an apostle.
readings: Read as a personal defense

Paul has been accused of fickleness, and 1:12–24 is a legal-sounding answer: he calls God as witness, appeals to his conscience, and shows that the changes in his plans were made for the Corinthians' good. On this reading the opening blessing is already part of the defense. Paul shows that his troubles have a purpose and that his word can be trusted because he has been through the fire.
Read as a theology of comfort

The first paragraph sets out a picture that governs the rest of the letter: God comforts the afflicted, so that they can comfort others. Suffering is not proof that God has left Paul, as his critics may have said, but the place where God's comfort is found and passed on. The defense of 1:12–24 then depends on this picture, since Paul's changed plans came from love, not weakness.

views.H: Paul writes from Macedonia, probably in the autumn of about AD 55 or 56 (dates vary by a year or two), to a Roman colony whose citizens prized honor, patronage and reliable speech. A patron who broke his word lost face, so the charge that Paul said "Yes" and "No" at once was serious. "Asia" is the province whose capital was Ephesus, where Paul had lived for two to three years (Acts 19:8, 10; 20:31). The sudden danger of 1:8–10 may be linked to the troubles there (Acts 19:23–41; 1 Corinthians 15:32; 16:9), but Paul does not say.
views.C: Paul and Timothy are named as senders, yet the letter is mostly in the first person, and scholars debate whether "we" means Paul alone. The chapter is the opening of what many take to be a letter pieced together from several: 1:1–2:13 joins smoothly to 7:5–16, and the long passage between them (2:14–7:4) can look like an interruption (Bornkamm), though Harris finds the whole to be one letter. Textual questions include "holiness" or "simplicity" at 1:12, the order of 1:6, and "therefore" at 1:20.
views.L: The blessing is a single long sentence in Greek (1:3–7), held together by repeated words: comfort (ten times) and suffering (four). Paul's "we" and "you" move back and forth, and he often says one thing in two ways ("trouble" and "death," "rescued" and "will rescue"). In 1:17–20 he plays on "Yes" and "No" and builds up to "Amen." The formal opening (1:1–2) uses the ordinary letter greeting with a Christian turn: the Greek greeting "grace" (charis) together with the Hebrew "peace" (shalom).
views.J: The letter opens with a Jewish blessing, barukh, not the Greek thanks found in most of Paul's letters. The titles for God ("Father of compassion," "God of all comfort") draw on the Hebrew Scriptures (Psalm 103:13; Isaiah 40:1; 51:12). "Amen" is the Hebrew response of a congregation to a prayer. "God who raises the dead" (1:9) matches the second blessing of the Jewish prayer called the Amidah, though that prayer's wording cannot be dated to Paul. Paul sees all God's promises as confirmed in Christ (1:20; Romans 15:8), a claim that Jewish readers dispute as a reading of the promises, while "Paul within Judaism" scholars stress that he still speaks of promises made to Israel.
views.T: Later readers have heard the Trinity in 1:21–22: God establishes and anoints us in Christ, seals us and gives the Spirit. The Mystagogical Catecheses, attributed to Cyril of Jerusalem or to his successor John, explain the anointing of the newly baptized with chrism (Catechesis 3). Catholic teaching sees the "seal" as the sacramental character (CCC 1121, 1274, 1295–1296), the Reformed see assurance (Westminster Confession 18.2), and Baptist and evangelical teachers often see the Spirit's gift at conversion.

deep.h: Paul and Corinth: the letters and visits
deep.b:
2 Corinthians is the fourth stage of a long conversation. The order below is a common reconstruction. The dates are approximate, and each step has been questioned.

  1. The founding visit (about AD 50–52). Paul stayed eighteen months in Corinth, working with Aquila and Priscilla and teaching in the house of Titius Justus. Silvanus and Timothy joined him (Acts 18:1–11; 2 Corinthians 1:19). Gallio's term as proconsul (known from an inscription at Delphi) fixes the end of this stay at about AD 51–52 (Acts 18:12).
  2. The earlier letter. Paul mentions a letter he wrote about avoiding immoral people (1 Corinthians 5:9). It is not preserved, unless part of it is in 2 Corinthians 6:14–7:1 (a theory, not a certainty).
  3. 1 Corinthians from Ephesus (about AD 54–55), answering reports from Chloe's people and a letter from Corinth (1 Corinthians 1:11; 7:1; 16:8). It announces a plan: Macedonia first, then Corinth (1 Corinthians 16:5–7).
  4. The painful visit. Probably a short trip from Ephesus, after which Paul says he will not come again "in grief" (2:1; 12:14; 13:2). Someone wronged him (2:5; 7:12).
  5. The tearful letter, most likely carried by Titus (2:3–4; 7:8–12). It may be lost; some think chapters 10–13 belong to it.
  6. Troas and Macedonia. Paul leaves Ephesus, finds no peace at Troas, and meets Titus in Macedonia, who brings good news (2:12–13; 7:5–16).
  7. 2 Corinthians, written from Macedonia (autumn of about AD 55 or 56). Paul announces a third visit (12:14; 13:1).
  8. The third visit, a stay of three months in Greece (Acts 20:2–3), during which Paul writes Romans from Corinth (Romans 16:1, 23) and prepares to take the collection to Jerusalem (Romans 15:25–27).

Acts mentions only the founding visit and the last visit. The reconstruction therefore depends on Paul's letters. A minority hold that there was no painful visit and that the tearful letter is 1 Corinthians. See the notes at 1:15–16 and 2:1–4.

deep.h: "Yes" and "No": why the changed plan mattered
deep.b: The charge in 1:17 is that Paul acts "by the flesh," that is, by merely human calculation, so that his "Yes" may turn into "No" when it suits him. In a city of patronage this mattered: a patron's word bound his dependents, and a teacher who broke his word could not expect to be trusted in other things. Paul's answer has three steps. (1) He appeals to God's faithfulness (1:18). (2) He says that his message about Jesus has the same shape: in Christ, God's answer to every promise is Yes (1:19–20). (3) He explains that his real reason was care: he stayed away "to spare you" (1:23), because another visit would have been in anger (2:1). Paul is saying that a pastor's change of plan may be a form of faithfulness.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the Corinthians' own "Amen" is part of the argument
deep.b:
Paul says that the "Amen" also goes up to God "through him" (1:20). In the first letter he takes for granted that a congregation says "Amen" at the end of a prayer (1 Corinthians 14:16). When Paul's letter was read aloud in the Corinthian assembly, the church would have said Amen to what it heard. If so, Paul's argument has a performance built in: as the listeners answer "Amen" to the promises read to them, they are doing what Paul has just said he and they do together, and they cannot easily say "Yes" to God's promises while treating Paul's own word as "Yes and No."

This is my own suggestion. It rests on 1:20 and 1 Corinthians 14:16. I have not seen the argument in this form in the commentaries I know, though many note that "Amen" is the church's liturgical response.

echoes: Psalm 41:13; Isaiah 40:1; Isaiah 51:12; Genesis 38:17–20; Matthew 5:37; James 5:12; Romans 4:17; Romans 15:8; 1 Corinthians 16:5–7; Acts 18:1–11; Acts 19:23–41; Acts 20:1–3; Ephesians 1:3; Ephesians 1:13–14

settings.to: The church of God in Corinth, and all the saints throughout Achaia: a mostly Gentile church of free people, slaves, a few wealthy patrons and many poor members, with believers in nearby towns such as Cenchreae
settings.when: Autumn of about AD 55 or 56, from Macedonia, soon after Titus brought news that the break with Corinth had begun to heal
settings.why: To say who is writing and with what authority, at a time when that authority was under question. Paul names himself an apostle "through the will of God" and not through the recommendation of the church, and he joins Timothy to the greeting because Timothy helped found the church and had been sent to them before.
settings.readers: The Corinthians themselves, and the Christians of Achaia who would hear the letter read, perhaps in house gatherings in several places.

settings.what: A blessing of God, and the story of the trouble in Asia
settings.to: The Corinthians, who knew of Paul's troubles only from rumor and may have taken them as a sign of God's disfavor
settings.when: At the head of the letter, looking back on the danger Paul had faced in Asia and the long worry over Corinth
settings.why: To tell them what had happened to him and to teach them how to read it: God comforts the afflicted so that they can comfort others. The prayer also asks for the Corinthians' own prayers (1:11), tying them to the outcome and drawing them back into partnership after the quarrel.
views: Some read 1:8–11 as meant for the whole of Achaia, since the letter was meant to circulate (1:1).
Others read it as directed at the Corinthians' scorn for an apostle who suffers: those who looked for power and success in a leader (compare 10:10) found Paul's weakness an embarrassment.

settings.what: A defense of his changed travel plans
settings.to: The Corinthians, some of whom had said he was unreliable
settings.when: After he had twice changed his plan to visit, and after the painful visit and the tearful letter
settings.why: To show that his decisions were made out of love and not out of calculation or fear, and to place his word inside God's own faithfulness. He wants them to see that staying away was his way of sparing them, and that he is a fellow worker for their joy, not a master over their faith.
settings.readers: A church whose honor culture read a broken promise as a loss of face; Paul answers in terms they would grasp (oath, witness, conscience).

traditions.q: What is the "seal" God puts on believers? (1:22)
views: The seal is a spiritual mark, the sacramental "character" given in baptism, confirmation and holy orders, which cannot be repeated (CCC 1121, 1274, 1295–1296).

In chrismation, the priest anoints the newly baptized with the words "the seal of the gift of the Holy Spirit." Cyril of Jerusalem's Catechetical Lecture 21 (Mystagogical Catechesis 3) explains the anointing, the "unction," to the newly baptized.

The Spirit's seal is God's pledge of salvation to the elect. It gives assurance that believers will receive their inheritance (Westminster Confession 18.2), and the sacraments are called signs and seals of the covenant of grace (Westminster Confession 27.1).

title: Grief, Forgiveness and the Victory Parade
sum: Chapter 2 continues Paul's explanation of why he did not come. He chose not to visit again in grief, and wrote instead "through many tears" (2:1–4). He then turns to a man in the church who had caused grief and been punished. Paul now asks the church to forgive him and to comfort him, lest he be swallowed up, and lest Satan gain an advantage (2:5–11). This is one of the New Testament's plainest pictures of church discipline and of its aim, which is to bring a person back.

Then the story stops. Paul went to Troas, found a door open, but could not rest because Titus had not come, and went on to Macedonia (2:12–13). At this point, instead of finishing the story, he breaks out in thanks: God leads him in a victory parade and spreads through him the scent of the knowledge of Christ, a sweet perfume to God, life to some and death to others (2:14–17). The question "who is up to this task?" opens the long defense of the ministry that follows in chapters 3 to 7.
readings: Read as one continuous letter

The break at 2:13 is deliberate. Paul is overcome by relief when he thinks of Titus, and he stops his story to thank God. He picks it up again at 7:5, with the same Macedonia and the same Titus. The long passage between is then a unit of its own, a defense of his ministry given while the reader waits for the news (defended by Harris).
Read as a join between two letters

2:13 and 7:5 fit so closely that some scholars (Bornkamm) think 2:14–7:4 was added from another letter, and that the editor put the thanksgiving at 2:14 to join the pieces. Others reply that nothing requires the break, and that a writer may leave a story for a time. The question matters for how the whole letter is read, and the two readings give the same words in different settings.

views.H: The Corinthians lived under a system of patronage and public honor. Church discipline was a delicate thing in such a city, since an offender might have a powerful friend; Paul speaks of the punishment as by "the majority" (2:6). Troas was the harbor from which one crossed to Macedonia, and the Roman triumph that Paul pictures in 2:14 was a familiar spectacle in the empire: the general in his chariot, captives in chains, and incense burning along the way.
views.C: Who is the offender (2:5–11)? The older view says he is the man of 1 Corinthians 5; most modern scholars say he wronged Paul himself. What letter is the "tearful letter" (2:3–4)? Is it lost, 1 Corinthians, or chapters 10–13? The break between 2:13 and 2:14, and the resumption at 7:5, are the strongest evidence for partition theories. Textual points: the Byzantine text reads "the rest" for "the many" at 2:17.
views.L: The thanks of 2:14 bursts in after an unfinished sentence. 2:14–16 is built on contrasts: triumph and captivity, life and death, sweet perfume and the smell of death. The rhetorical question "who is able?" (2:16) leads straight into 3:5, "our ability comes from God." Paul uses a rare verb for peddling (2:17), and it prepares for the contrast between his own sincerity and the "letters of introduction" that others carry (3:1).
views.J: Forgiveness and restoration after discipline match Jewish practice: a person who repents is received back, and the community is warned against a harshness that drives a sinner to despair (compare Sirach 28:1–7 on forgiving a neighbor). The images of 2:15–16 are drawn from sacrifice: the "soothing aroma" that rises from an offering (Genesis 8:21; Leviticus 1:9). The saying that Torah is a drug of life or of death (Yoma 72b) is a later parallel to the double effect of a word from God.
views.T: The discipline in 2:5–11 is the pattern used for the later practice of penance. Catholic teaching reads the "in the person of Christ" of the Latin text as the basis for absolution by a priest (Trent, session 14; CCC 1461). Reformed and Baptist teachers read it as congregational restoration. Early writers often took the triumph of 2:14 as Christ's victory over death and the powers (compare Colossians 2:15).

deep.b:
Paul's counsel is shaped like a short course in church discipline. (1) A wrong was done, and the church acted: "this punishment from the majority" (2:6). (2) The offender repented. (3) Paul asks the church to reverse course and to "confirm" its love in a formal act (2:8): the Greek verb kyroo is a legal word for ratifying a decision. (4) The danger now is on the other side: too much severity ("swallowed up by too much grief," 2:7). (5) Paul joins the church in the act (2:10): "Anyone you forgive anything, I forgive too."

The earlier case, in 1 Corinthians 5:1–5, ended with the man being handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit might be saved. Whether the two cases are one is argued (see the note at 2:5). The pattern is the same in either: severity is for the sinner's recovery, and the church that will not forgive gives Satan an opening (2:11).

deep.h: The Roman triumph and Paul's picture (2:14–16)
deep.b:
A triumph was the highest honor a Roman general could receive. The army marched through the city to the Capitol, with the general in a chariot, wearing a purple robe, his soldiers singing, his captives in chains, and incense rising from altars and braziers along the way. At the end, the chief enemy leader was often put to death. Josephus describes the triumph of Vespasian and Titus after the Jewish War, in which the captive leader Simon was dragged to the forum and killed (Jewish War 7.121–157).

Paul's picture has three possible casts for "us": captives led to death, soldiers sharing the glory, or people through whom the victor spreads his fame. The rest of the letter favors the first, where Paul's weakness, danger and "dying" (4:7–12; 11:23–33) are the proof that Christ is the victor, not Paul. The perfume supplies the second half of the picture: the same smell is life to the saved and death to the lost. The Plain says "victory parade" so that all three readings remain open.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the incense of the Day of Atonement lies behind the "smell of death and life"
deep.b:
The usual source suggested for the perfume of 2:14–16 is the Roman triumph. A second possible source is the incense of the Day of Atonement. The high priest was to put incense on the fire "so that he does not die" (Leviticus 16:13): the cloud of incense covered the atonement lid, and it protected the priest from death. In this picture the same smoke is death for one who enters without it, and life for one who enters with it. Paul has just asked "who is up to this task?", a priest's question (2:16), and Paul's "we are the sweet perfume of Christ" (2:15) puts the apostles in the position of the smoke between God and the people.

This is my own suggestion and not a settled reading. It fits the "soothing aroma" of sacrifice that some commentators find in 2:15 (Genesis 8:21; Leviticus 1:9), but I have not seen it tied to Leviticus 16:13 in this way in the commentaries I know. Against it: Paul does not mention the Day of Atonement here.

echoes: Genesis 8:21; Leviticus 1:9; Leviticus 16:13; 1 Corinthians 5:1–5; 1 Corinthians 16:9; Colossians 2:15; Colossians 4:3; Acts 16:8–11; Acts 20:5–12; 2 Corinthians 7:5–16; Matthew 18:15–18; Sirach 28:1–7

settings.what: On grief, the offender and forgiveness
settings.to: The Corinthian church as a whole, which had punished an offender "by the majority" while a minority may have disagreed
settings.when: After Titus returned with news that the church had acted against the offender
settings.why: To explain why he wrote the tearful letter (to show his love and to test their obedience), and to ask them to end the discipline with forgiveness. Too much severity could harm the man and give Satan a way into the church. Paul puts his own forgiveness beside theirs so that the church does not feel that he is overruling them.
views: The older view takes him to be the man who lived with his father's wife, repentant now.
Most modern scholars take him to be someone who insulted Paul or his delegate at the painful visit (7:12).

settings.what: The journey to Troas and Macedonia
settings.when: On the road from Ephesus, looking for Titus
settings.why: To show how much he cared. He left a ministry that was open because he could not rest without news from Corinth. The story is also meant to ease them: they need not think that Paul has written them off.

settings.what: Thanks for the victory parade, and the sweet perfume of Christ
settings.to: The Corinthians, among whom some were comparing Paul with preachers they thought more impressive
settings.when: At the pivot of the letter, the turn from the story of travel to the defense of his ministry
settings.why: To give a reason for what looks like weakness. If apostles are led in the victory parade as captives, their hardships are part of the procession of Christ, not evidence against it. The "peddlers" he contrasts with himself are rivals (or Corinthian ideas of how a teacher ought to act) who treat God's word as goods for sale.

traditions.q: Who can pronounce God's forgiveness on a sinner? (2:10)
views: Christ entrusted the power of absolution to the apostolic ministry, and bishops and priests continue it in the sacrament of penance (Council of Trent, session 14, chapter 6; CCC 1442, 1461).
Private confession and absolution are kept in the churches (Augsburg Confession 11 and 25).

The keys of the kingdom are the preaching of the gospel and Christian discipline (Heidelberg Catechism 83-85; compare Westminster Confession 30, on church censures). By discipline a person who will not repent is shut out, and a person who shows amendment is received again.
The congregation disciplines a member who falls into sin: he is admonished twice in private, and if the offense is repeated he is openly disciplined and put under the ban (Schleitheim Confession).

title: A Letter Written on Hearts, and the Veil
sum: Paul has just asked, "who is up to this task?" He begins to answer by asking whether he must again vouch for himself with letters of introduction, as some others do. His letter, he says, is the Corinthian church itself, written on his heart and read by all, written not in ink but by the Spirit of the living God, not on stone but on hearts of flesh (3:1–3). The language is taken from Jeremiah's new covenant and Ezekiel's new heart. God has made Paul able to serve that covenant, "not of the letter but of the Spirit" (3:4–6).

From 3:7 Paul compares two ministries by going back to Exodus 34, where Moses's face shone and he covered it with a veil. If the ministry carved on stone had glory, the ministry of the Spirit has far more. The veil that Moses wore becomes a picture of a veil over the mind of those who read Moses without turning to the Lord (3:14–16). When one turns, the veil is removed, and all believers, with uncovered faces, are changed into the image of the Lord "from glory to glory" (3:18). This is the most disputed chapter in the letter for Jewish–Christian relations.
readings: Read as a contrast between Judaism and Christianity

The traditional Christian reading takes the chapter as setting the old religion of the Law against the new religion of the Spirit. The old covenant kills, is fading and is veiled; the new gives life, remains and is open. On this reading the Jewish people, as readers of Moses, still have the veil on their minds until they turn to Christ (a common reading from the Fathers into the twentieth century).
Read as a contrast between two ministries

Many scholars today hold that Paul is not comparing Judaism with Christianity but Moses's ministry with his own. The Sinai ministry (with Exodus 32–34 behind it) ended in judgment on a hard-hearted people, while the ministry of the Spirit gives the heart that obeys. The veil is a picture of a hardness that remains until anyone, Jew or Gentile, turns to the Lord (Hafemann). Paul still honors the Law (Romans 7:12) and still hopes for Israel (Romans 11:26).
Read as a defense of Paul against rivals

A third reading begins with 3:1 and the rivals who carried letters and boasted of their Jewish credentials (11:22). Paul is answering them in terms they would understand, and the chapter says little about Judaism as such (Georgi, with differences). On this reading, the question of how Jews and Christians relate must be answered from other texts, such as Romans 9–11.

views.H: Letters of recommendation were ordinary in the Greek world and the church (Acts 18:27; Romans 16:1–2). Stone tablets for law and public decrees were a familiar sight in a Greek city, as were mirrors of polished bronze (Corinth was known for its bronze work, and some wonder whether that lies behind Paul's picture in 3:18, though he does not say so). The letter to the Corinthians is written in an honor culture, where the apostle's credentials mattered, and where arrivals from Judea, with their letters and their claims, could outshine Paul.
views.C: The chapter is full of argued points. Does "letter" mean the Law, the literal sense, or the written code of Moses's covenant (3:6)? Does "fading" mean the glory faded, or that it was set aside (3:7–14)? Is "the Lord is the Spirit" an identification of persons, or an exegetical remark on Exodus 34:34 (3:17)? Is "mirror" looking or reflecting (3:18)? Many see 3:7–18 as a unit with its own structure, and Georgi suggests that Paul is reworking his rivals' own teaching on Moses. The Textus Receptus reads "of a heart" for "hearts" at 3:3.
views.L: The chapter uses "lesser to greater" arguments (3:7–8, 9, 11), a form that Jewish teachers called qal va-chomer. It runs on pairs: ink and Spirit, stone and flesh, letter and Spirit, death and life, condemnation and righteousness, fading and remaining. The word "glory" (doxa) comes ten times. The veil, which is a fact of Exodus 34, is turned into a figure of the mind (3:14–15), and then into the removal of the covering (3:16, 18). The chapter ends with a verb that sums up the letter's hope: "are being changed" (3:18).
views.J: Paul draws on the Hebrew prophets (Jeremiah 31:31–34; Ezekiel 36:26–27) for a hope that God would write the Torah on the heart, which Jewish readers have taken as a hope for Israel's faithful keeping of the same Torah, not for another law. Jewish readers have also pointed out that Exodus 34 gives no hint that the glory faded, and that Paul's reading of the veil goes beyond the text. "Paul within Judaism" scholars stress that Paul is talking to Gentiles about their own situation.
views.T: Origen used 3:6 to defend finding a spiritual meaning behind the literal text of Scripture (On First Principles 4). Augustine, in On the Spirit and the Letter (AD 412), made it central to his doctrine of grace: the letter commands, the Spirit gives the power. Aquinas (Summa Theologiae I-II q.106) calls the New Law chiefly the grace of the Holy Spirit. Luther made it the center of the distinction of law and gospel. Calvin (Institutes 2.11) used it to compare the testaments while insisting on one covenant of grace. Gregory of Nyssa read "from glory to glory" as the soul's endless ascent (Life of Moses), and Eastern theology reads 3:18 as theosis.

deep.h: Exodus 34 and Paul's reading, side by side
deep.b:
Paul retells the story of Exodus 34:29–35 with several points that the Hebrew does not make. This table sets out what Exodus says and what Paul adds.

  • Exodus 34:29–30: the skin of Moses's face shone, and the people were afraid to come near. Paul (3:7): they "could not look steadily" because of the glory.
  • Exodus 34:33: Moses put on a veil after speaking to the people. Paul (3:13): he did so "so that the Israelites would not look steadily at the end of what was being set aside." Exodus gives no such reason.
  • Exodus 34:34: whenever Moses went in before the LORD, he took the veil off. Paul (3:16): "whenever someone turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away."
  • Exodus: says nothing of the glory fading. Paul: says it was "being set aside" (3:7, 11, 13).
  • Exodus 32:28; 33:3: the golden calf, three thousand dead, and God's refusal to go with them lest he destroy them. Paul (3:7, 9): the ministry of "death" and "condemnation." This is the background many scholars see.

Paul is therefore doing what Jewish interpreters of his day did: reading a story with the questions of the present in mind (compare the pesher readings of Qumran). The question for the reader is whether the added details are accurate readings of the logic of the story, or Paul's own application. Jewish readers often say the second.

deep.h: How the letter and the Spirit have been read
deep.b: The pair "letter and Spirit" in 3:6 has generated a long history of reading. Origen took the "letter" as the plain sense of Scripture, which can kill if read without insight, and the "Spirit" as the deeper sense: a view that shaped medieval exegesis. Augustine (AD 412) argued that the letter is the law without the grace that makes keeping it possible, so that the letter kills by showing guilt and the Spirit gives life by love. Luther read it as law and gospel. Calvin read it as the Law considered apart from the Spirit's work and kept the unity of the covenant of grace. Modern scholarship since Hafemann (1995) has returned to the Exodus background: the "letter" is the written code of Sinai that, without a new heart, condemned a hard-hearted people, and the Spirit is the promised gift of Jeremiah and Ezekiel. A last group, some "Paul within Judaism" readers, reads the chapter as a contrast between Paul's own mission to Gentiles and the stricter claims of his opponents, not a contrast between the faiths.

deep.h: "Old covenant" and the question of supersession
deep.b: Supersession is the idea that the church has replaced Israel as God's people and that the covenant with Israel is over. The phrase "old covenant" in 3:14 is often cited for it, as is Hebrews 8:13, where the first covenant is "obsolete." Three observations bear on the question. (1) Paul does not use "old" to mean "cancelled": he says the veil stays "when the old covenant is read," so the reading, not the covenant, is where the problem lies. (2) In Romans 9–11 Paul says the gifts and calling of God are not taken back (Romans 11:29) and that "all Israel will be saved" (Romans 11:26). (3) The weight of 2 Corinthians 3 falls on the two ministries and on the glory, not on the fate of the Jewish people. After the Holocaust many churches re-examined the teaching of supersession (Nostra Aetate 4, 1965; the ELCA declaration of 1994). The cards on this page set out how the traditions answer.

deep.title: Claude's theory: Moses is the pattern for "turning to the Lord"
deep.b:
In Exodus 34:34 Moses goes in before the LORD, takes off the veil, speaks with God, and comes out. Paul uses Moses's practice as the pattern for every believer: "whenever someone turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away" (3:16). The verse then reads as if Moses were the first person to go through the experience that Paul describes for all, and as if the veil of 3:13 were not only a cover for his face but a picture of the covering Moses took off each time he went in. On this reading Moses is not a figure on the other side of the line, as 3:14–15 can suggest, but the first of those who turn.

This is a suggestion of my own. It overlaps in part with readings that take 3:16 as a direct application of Exodus 34:34 (for example Hafemann), but I have not seen a commentary that builds the chapter's two sides on it in just this way.

echoes: Exodus 24:12; Exodus 31:18; Exodus 32:19; Exodus 32:28; Exodus 33:3; Exodus 34:1; Exodus 34:29–35; Jeremiah 31:31–34; Ezekiel 11:19–20; Ezekiel 36:26–27; Deuteronomy 30:6; Romans 2:29; Romans 7:6; Romans 7:12; Romans 8:2; Romans 10:4; Romans 11:7–12; Romans 11:25–29; Galatians 4:24; 1 Corinthians 11:25; 1 Corinthians 13:12; Hebrews 8:6–13

settings.what: The church as Paul's letter of recommendation
settings.to: The Corinthians, among whom rivals carried letters of introduction
settings.when: After the defense of 2:14–17, in answer to the suspicion that he was boasting
settings.why: To say that no outside document is needed to prove his apostleship: the Corinthians themselves, changed by the gospel, are the proof. The pictures from Jeremiah and Ezekiel (hearts, Spirit, flesh) prepare for the contrast of 3:6–18.
settings.readers: A church that had been taught to value written credentials and public honor; the answer is that the best evidence of an apostle is a changed community.

settings.what: The ministry of the new covenant and the veil of Moses
settings.to: The Corinthians, a mostly Gentile church that heard Moses read, and that was being told by others that it needed Jewish credentials
settings.when: At the center of the defense of his ministry (2:14–7:4)
settings.why: To show that his ministry, the ministry of the Spirit, is glorious beyond that of Moses, and that his open speech (3:12) follows from it. He draws a picture of the Sinai covenant as a covenant of letters that could not change hearts, and of the new covenant as the Spirit's work in them, promised in Jeremiah 31. He also says why some do not accept the gospel: a veil lies on the reading of Moses.
settings.readers: Gentile believers who had little knowledge of how Jews read the Law, and Jewish believers in the church; and perhaps visitors who argued from Moses (11:22).
views: The traditional view: Paul sets the Mosaic covenant against the new.
Paul compares Moses's ministry with his own, within one story of God's dealing with Israel (Hafemann).
Paul answers rivals who claimed Moses's authority (Georgi).

traditions.q: What does "the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life" mean? (3:6)
views: Aquinas, following Augustine, takes "the letter" as any external writing, even the Gospel's, which would kill without the inward grace of faith, and says the New Law is chiefly the grace of the Holy Spirit (Summa Theologiae I-II, q.106). The Old Law is a preparation for the Gospel (CCC 1961-1964).

The Law is a ministration that kills through the letter and preaches condemnation (2 Corinthians 3:7), and the Gospel is the power of God to salvation and gives the Spirit. The right distinction of Law and Gospel is central to Lutheran teaching (Formula of Concord, Solid Declaration, article 5).

There is one covenant of grace in two administrations, the Old Testament and the New (Westminster Confession 7.5-6), and the law remains a rule of life for believers who are not under it as a covenant of works (19.6).
Wesley's Notes take "the letter" as the law, the Mosaic dispensation, which "kills" those who cling to it, and "the Spirit" as the gospel, which is written on the heart by the Spirit.
Mark Kinzer, in Postmissionary Messianic Judaism (2005), argues against supersessionist theology and for a Torah-observant Messianic Judaism.
Dispensationalists differ on the new covenant: some hold that its promises to Israel will be fulfilled for Israel at the beginning of the Millennium, while the Church shares in it now.

traditions.q: Is the covenant with Israel through Moses ended? (3:14–16)
views: The Old Covenant "has never been revoked" (CCC 121), and God "does not repent of the gifts He makes or of the calls He issues" (Nostra Aetate 4).

Lutheran teaching distinguishes Law and Gospel. Moses read alone accuses, and the veil lies on the heart until the Gospel of Christ lifts it (Formula of Concord, Solid Declaration 5). Luther's late writing On the Jews and Their Lies (1543) was rejected in 1994 by the Church Council of the Evangelical Lutheran Church in America, which called its violent invective something "we reject."

There is one covenant of grace in different administrations, the Old Testament and the New (Westminster Confession 7.5-6): "There are not, therefore, two covenants of grace differing in substance, but one and the same under various dispensations."
Mark Kinzer's Postmissionary Messianic Judaism (2005) seeks to refute supersessionist theology.

traditions.q: What does "from glory to glory" mean for the Christian life? (3:18)
views: Gregory of Nyssa describes growth toward God as a continual stretching forward (epektasis). Gregory Palamas defended the uncreated character of the light of the Transfiguration and the distinction between God's essence and energies. Athanasius, On the Incarnation 54, speaks of the Word's "deifying mission."

Grace is a participation in the life of God (CCC 1997); it is "the sanctifying or deifying grace received in Baptism" (CCC 1999), and the Word became man so that we might become "partakers of the divine nature" (CCC 460).

Tuomo Mannermaa and the "new Finnish interpretation of Luther" present Luther's views on salvation in terms much closer to the Eastern Orthodox doctrine of theosis than established German Luther scholarship does.
Believers are sanctified "really and personally" through the virtue of Christ's death and resurrection, by his Word and Spirit dwelling in them (Westminster Confession 13.1).

title: Treasure in Clay Pots
sum: Having this ministry, Paul says, he does not give up. He has given up secrets and tricks, and states the truth openly. If the good news is still covered by a veil for some, it is because "the god of this age" has blinded the minds of those who do not believe, so that they cannot see the light of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God (4:1–4). Paul preaches Christ as Lord and himself as the church's slave. The God who said "Light will shine out of darkness" has shone in his heart (4:5–6).

Then comes one of the letter's best-known images: this treasure is held in clay pots, so that the overwhelming power is God's (4:7). Four pairs of hardships follow, each matched with a limit (4:8–9). Paul carries the dying of Jesus in his body so that the life of Jesus may be shown in it (4:10–12). He ends with hope: the God who raised Jesus will raise him, and the outer person is falling apart but the inner is renewed, and the trouble that is slight and short is producing a glory beyond measure that lasts forever (4:13–18).
readings: Read as Paul's own story

The chapter is Paul's description of his life as an apostle: the danger in Asia (1:8–10), the daily pressures, and his hope. The "dying" and the "life" are literal: he is often near death, and the church receives life through his labors. Seen this way the chapter is the center of the letter's picture of an apostle who is weak and yet effective.
Read as a picture of every believer

Though Paul writes first about the apostolic ministry, the language has been taken to apply to every Christian: the treasure is the gospel in each believer, the pots are ordinary human lives, and the pairs of hardship and rescue are the pattern of the Christian life. The text itself moves from "we" the apostles to "we" all (4:13–14, 16–18). Both uses have a long history in preaching.

views.H: Clay jars were everywhere in the ancient world: cheap, breakable, used for water, oil, wine and for storing documents (Jeremiah 32:14). A triumph, a hardship list and the shame of a weak leader would all have been familiar images. Paul's list of hardships is much like the lists a Stoic teacher wrote to show that the wise man cannot be shaken, with the difference that Paul does not claim immunity (Fitzgerald).
views.C: Does "the god of this age" mean Satan, or God (Irenaeus and Tertullian read it as God, against Marcion)? Is the light of 4:6 an allusion to Genesis 1:3, to Isaiah 9:2, or to Paul's conversion? Is "clay pots" an image of the body or of the apostle's life? Textual points: "Jesus Christ" or "Christ" at 4:6; "the Lord Jesus" at 4:10 and "through" for "with" at 4:14 in the Textus Receptus, and "light will shine" or "commanded light to shine" at 4:6.
views.L: The chapter is built from antitheses, a form that makes paradox plain: "squeezed, but not crushed." The four pairs of 4:8–9 are a poem. 4:10–12 states the pattern in plain prose (death in us, life in you). 4:16–18 sets up a scale, with "slight" and "momentary" trouble on one side and a "weight" of glory on the other. The quotation of Psalm 116:10 in 4:13 gives the passage its ground: speech comes from faith. Words for sight and the unseen mark the end (4:18).
views.J: The "god of this age" belongs to the Jewish picture of two ages and a hostile power over the present one (compare the Angel of Darkness in the Qumran Community Rule, 1QS 3:20–24, as a parallel in thought). Psalm 116 is part of the Hallel sung at Passover, so Paul quotes a psalm that his readers might have known in worship. The clay pots recall Jeremiah's earthen vessel (Jeremiah 32:14) and the potter's clay (Isaiah 64:8; Jeremiah 18). "Light out of darkness" echoes Genesis 1:3 and the "light" of Isaiah (9:2; 60:1–3).
views.T: Irenaeus (Against Heresies 3.7.1) and Tertullian (Against Marcion 5.11) read it as saying that God has blinded the unbelievers, to block Marcion's use. Calvin and Luther took it as Satan.

deep.h: Hardship lists and the apostle's weakness
deep.b:
Paul gives four lists of this kind in the letter: 4:8–9, 6:4–10, 11:23–29 and 12:10. Hardship lists (peristaseis) were a known form; Stoic teachers, such as Seneca in Paul's day and Epictetus a generation later, listed the troubles the wise man bears without being shaken, to show that the wise man is free. Paul borrows the form and changes it in four ways. (1) He is not above the troubles: he is squeezed and knocked down. (2) The limits are not in his own strength but in God ("not crushed" is a statement about God's care). (3) The troubles are a part of his message, not a sign that it fails: "the dying of Jesus" is carried "in the body" (4:10). (4) The purpose is for others: "death works in us, and life in you" (4:12).

Paul's critics in Corinth wanted a leader who showed power, eloquence and success. His answer, in this chapter and in chapters 10–13, is that the cross is the shape of his ministry and not an embarrassment to it (see 12:9, where Christ's power is made perfect in weakness). Fitzgerald's book on these lists, Cracks in an Earthen Vessel, takes its title from 4:7.

deep.h: Who is "the god of this age"?
deep.b: The plain reading is that Paul means Satan. Paul has already named him in 2:11, and he will do so again (11:3, 14; 12:7). Two ideas lie behind the phrase "this age." The first is the Jewish picture of two ages, the present evil age and the age to come (Galatians 1:4), where the present one has a ruler. The second is Paul's own picture of the cross as the turn of the ages (1 Corinthians 2:6–8; Galatians 1:4). Because the phrase "god of this age" is not found elsewhere in Paul, some early Christians took "God" as the subject of the blinding (Irenaeus, Tertullian). The reason was not that the grammar demands it but that Marcion and the Gnostics used the verse to say that the Creator was a lesser or evil god. Paul can call Satan a "god" in the sense that he has power over what people worship and trust (compare 1 Corinthians 8:5; Philippians 3:19), without granting him deity. The churches that name him as Satan agree that his power is real but limited by God. The Catholic Catechism calls him a creature whose power is not infinite and who acts only as God permits (CCC 395, 2851–2854), and the Westminster Confession teaches that God's providence reaches even the sins of angels and men, with a wise and powerful bounding and governing of them (5.4).

deep.title: Claude's theory: the clay pots echo the sealed jar of Jeremiah 32
deep.b:
The usual background for "treasure in clay pots" is the ordinary use of clay jars to store valuables. A closer background may be Jeremiah 32:14, where Jeremiah buys a field at Anathoth while the Babylonians besiege Jerusalem and puts the deed of purchase in a clay jar "so that they will last for many days." The deed is a promise of return (Jeremiah 32:15) kept in a jar during the siege. In 2 Corinthians 4, Paul, who uses Jeremiah 31 in chapter 3, may have the next chapter of the same prophet in mind: the treasure is the promise of the new covenant, stored in a breakable jar during a time of siege.

This is my own suggestion. It fits the way chapter 3 uses Jeremiah 31 and the letter's emphasis on the promise kept through danger. I have not seen 4:7 tied to Jeremiah 32:14 in this way in the commentaries I know, though some may have made the link, and many cite the verse as an example of storage in jars.

echoes: Genesis 1:3; Isaiah 9:2; Isaiah 60:1–3; Psalm 112:4; Psalm 116:10; Jeremiah 32:14; Job 10:9; Isaiah 64:8; Romans 8:18; Romans 8:35–39; Galatians 6:17; Philippians 3:10; Colossians 1:15; 1 Corinthians 4:9–13; 1 Corinthians 15:42–49; John 12:31; Ephesians 2:2

settings.what: An open ministry, and why some do not see
settings.to: The Corinthians, some of whom suspected him of cunning, and some of whom were not persuaded by the gospel
settings.when: As the first part of the answer to "who is up to this task?" (2:16), after the picture of the two ministries in chapter 3
settings.why: To show that the way he works is open and honest, and that if the gospel is hidden from some, the cause is a veil and a blindness, not a defect in the message or the messenger. He also says what he preaches: not himself, but Jesus Christ as Lord.

settings.what: Treasure in clay pots, and hope beyond trouble
settings.to: The Corinthians, many of whom were uncomfortable with an apostle who suffered so much
settings.when: Within the defense of his ministry, soon after Paul's own near-death in Asia (1:8–10)
settings.why: To explain his weakness as a means: the power at work is God's, and so it shows best in a weak vessel. It also gives them hope: Paul's suffering is on their behalf, and he is not despairing, because he looks beyond what is seen to what lasts.
settings.readers: A church of people with their own troubles, who could read the passage as a comfort as well as a defense of the apostle.

title: The Tent, the Judgment and the New Creation
sum: Chapter 5 begins with Paul's hope for what lies beyond death. The body is a tent, and if it is taken down, God has a building ready, a house not made by human hands (5:1). Paul groans in the tent and longs to be "dressed over" with his heavenly home, not to be found unclothed. God has prepared him for this and has given him the Spirit as a down payment (5:2–5). So he is confident, even though to be at home in the body is to be away from the Lord, and he would prefer to be with the Lord. His ambition, either way, is to please him, because all must appear before the judgment seat of Christ (5:6–10).

From 5:11 the subject changes to the ministry that flows from this. Knowing the fear of the Lord, Paul tries to persuade people. The love of Christ holds him in its grip, because one died for all and so all died (5:14–15). That changes how he sees everyone, and Christ himself (5:16). If anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation (5:17). All this comes from God, who reconciled us to himself in Christ and gave us the ministry of reconciliation. The apostles are ambassadors who beg, "Be reconciled to God" (5:18–20). The chapter ends with one of the shortest and most debated sentences in the New Testament, on the exchange that made it possible (5:21).
readings: Read as hope for the dead and the dying

The first ten verses are Paul's personal hope, written after he had thought he might die (1:8–10). He does not want to be found without a body, and he is confident that he will be with the Lord. Reading it this way, the passage is mainly a pastoral comfort for people facing death, and it should be read with 1 Corinthians 15 and Philippians 1:21–23.
Read as the ground of the ministry

The whole of the chapter belongs to the argument of 2:14–7:4. Paul's confidence in the resurrection (5:1–10) is why he does not lose heart (4:1, 16), and the judgment of 5:10 is why he serves with sincerity (5:11). The new creation and reconciliation (5:14–21) are the content of what he preaches and the reason he preaches it. On this reading 5:1–10 is not a digression on the afterlife but part of the letter's defense.

views.H: The "tent" had a ready meaning for a tentmaker (Acts 18:3) and for readers who knew that the body is a tent in Wisdom of Solomon 9:15, a book that Catholic and Orthodox Christians count as Scripture. The Corinthian forum had a bema where magistrates sat. The ambassador (presbeutes) was a recognized figure in the Roman Empire, one who spoke for a ruler. Greek ideas of the soul as free of the body were in the air in Corinth, and some of the church's difficulties with resurrection (1 Corinthians 15) came from them.
views.C: Did Paul change his mind about the resurrection between 1 Corinthians 15 and 2 Corinthians 5 (Dodd's proposal that near-death in Asia moved him from hoping to be alive at Christ's coming to expecting to die)? What is the "building" and when is it received? What is the textual question at 5:3 ("clothed" or "unclothed")? What does "know no one by the flesh" (5:16) mean? What is the sense of "new creation" (5:17), and is it an individual, a community, or the cosmos? What does "to be sin" mean (5:21)? Textual points: "all things" at 5:17 (Textus Receptus, Byzantine) and "put on" or "taken off" at 5:3.
views.L: The sentence structure is dense: 5:1–4 is a chain of images (tent, building, clothing, swallowing). The words "at home" and "away" make a pun on citizenship (5:6–9). The central section 5:14–21 is built on the word "all" and on a series of exchanges: one for all, death for life, sin for righteousness. The key word "reconcile" and its relatives appear five times in three verses (5:18–20). The chapter closes with a climax in one of the shortest of Paul's pictures of the cross (5:21), a single sentence with a parallel structure.
views.J: The tent and the building are images found in Jewish texts about the body and the Temple, and the hope for resurrection was held by the Pharisees (Acts 23:6). The body as clothing that is put off and on is an old picture (Genesis 3:21). "New creation" appears in Jewish writings of the period (Jubilees 4:26 and 1 Enoch 72:1, which are Scripture for the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo church; 2 Baruch 32:6), and Isaiah's "new things" (43:19; 65:17) lie behind 5:17. The "ambassador" and "reconciliation" belong to the language of diplomacy, but 5:21 draws on the sin offering and the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 4; 16; Isaiah 53). Jewish readers point out that Judaism has its own teaching on atonement through repentance and the Day itself, and does not need a substitute.
views.T: For the Fathers and for the Reformation churches, 5:1–10 was a main text on the soul after death and on judgment according to works. The Catholic Church uses 5:10 for the particular and the last judgment (CCC 1021–1022, 1038–1041). Calvin used the passage against soul sleep (Psychopannychia, 1542). 5:14–21 was a battleground over the atonement: Anselm's satisfaction, Luther's "happy exchange," Calvin's substitution, the Fathers' victory over death and theosis, and Wesley's emphasis on the righteousness of Christ.

deep.h: Between death and resurrection: what 5:1–10 says and does not say
deep.b:
This is the most discussed paragraph in the letter on the afterlife. It raises four questions.

  1. What is the "building from God"? The main answers: the resurrection body, a heavenly body given at death (Harris, in his 1971 Tyndale lecture), the church as the corporate body of Christ (proposed by some), or heaven itself as a dwelling.
  2. When is it received? Paul's own words in 1 Corinthians 15:51–54 suggest at Christ's return, when the dead are raised and the living changed. In 2 Corinthians 5 he speaks as though he expects to die first. Dodd proposed that Paul's view developed after the danger in Asia (1:8–10); others hold that he did not change his mind and that he is speaking of the same hope with a new emphasis on the time between.
  3. What is the "unclothed" state (5:3–4)? Paul fears it, which suggests that a bodiless existence is not his hope. Yet he says he would prefer to be "away from the body and at home with the Lord" (5:8), and in Philippians 1:23 he longs "to depart and be with Christ." So the "unclothed" state may be the time of being with the Lord before the resurrection, a state he regards as better than life now but not the final goal.
  4. Is the dead person conscious? The Fathers and most churches say yes. Some traditions (Seventh-day Adventists, Jehovah's Witnesses) say that the dead are asleep or in a state in which time does not pass for them.

Paul does not answer all these questions, and the passage is better read as a statement of hope than a map of the afterlife. See the card for the churches' views.

The paragraph is a chain of steps, each resting on the one before. (1) The love of Christ holds Paul, because he has concluded that one died for all and so all died (5:14). (2) The purpose of his death: that the living no longer live for themselves (5:15). (3) A new way of seeing: no one, and not Christ, is known by the flesh (5:16). (4) New creation (5:17). (5) All of it is from God, who reconciled (5:18) and was reconciling the world, not counting trespasses (5:19). (6) Ambassadors carry the appeal (5:20). (7) The exchange that makes the appeal possible (5:21).

The movement is from the cross, to a new way of knowing, to a new world, to a mission, and back to the cross. Reconciliation here is not a mood but a transaction in which God is the actor. The word "reconcile" is Paul's own word for it, found in only a few places, and it describes a change in the relation between God and the world.

deep.h: "The righteousness of God" and the exchange of 5:21
deep.b:
Romans 3:21–26 uses "the righteousness of God" for God's own saving justice. In 2 Corinthians 5:21 believers "become" it. Four explanations are given. (1) Imputation: God counts Christ's righteousness as theirs, as he counted their sins as Christ's (the Reformed and Lutheran reading, using Romans 4). (2) Infusion: God makes them truly righteous by grace (the Catholic reading, Trent session 6). (3) The ministry: Paul and his co-workers, as apostles, embody God's covenant faithfulness as they carry the message of reconciliation (Wright's reading, based on the "we" in 5:20–21). (4) Participation: being "in him" is a share in the life of Christ, in whom the believer is joined to the righteousness of God (Orthodox, and Gorman and others).

The first half of the sentence is just as disputed. "To be sin" has been understood as sin offering, as sin bearing, or as exchange; see the note. The text says that Christ "did not know sin" and does not say he became a sinner. All the traditions agree on that point.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the "exchange" of 5:21 is built to answer the "exchange" of 3:18
deep.b:
In 3:18 believers are "changed into the same image" as they look at the Lord's glory. In 5:21 they "become the righteousness of God." Both verses speak of a change that happens to people "in" or by looking at the Lord. Between them stands the hardship of chapter 4, where Paul's "dying" brings life to others. A reader may see a three-step pattern: first a change by seeing the glory (3:18), then a change worked out in suffering (4:10–12), then a change worked by an exchange at the cross (5:21). If so, 5:21 is not a loose doctrinal summary but the ground of what chapters 3 and 4 describe.

This is my own suggestion. It overlaps with Gorman's reading of 2 Corinthians as about participation in Christ's pattern, but I have not seen the three verses set in this sequence in the commentaries I know.

echoes: Genesis 3:7; Genesis 3:21; Genesis 8:21; Isaiah 38:12; Isaiah 43:18–19; Isaiah 53:4–10; Isaiah 65:17; Leviticus 4:3; Leviticus 16:21–22; Psalm 32:1–2; Mark 14:58; Luke 23:43; Romans 3:21–26; Romans 4:6–8; Romans 5:10–11; Romans 6:3–8; Romans 8:3; Romans 14:10–12; Galatians 3:13; Galatians 6:15; Philippians 1:21–23; Colossians 1:19–22; 1 Corinthians 15:42–54; Wisdom of Solomon 9:15; 2 Maccabees 1:5; 2 Maccabees 7:33; Jubilees 4:26; 1 Enoch 72:1

settings.what: The hope of a heavenly dwelling, and the judgment seat
settings.to: The Corinthians, some of whom doubted the resurrection of the body (1 Corinthians 15) and many of whom thought of suffering as failure
settings.when: After the account of his near-death in Asia and of the hardships of 4:7–12
settings.why: To tell them why he is not discouraged. The body is a tent, and he has a hope beyond it. This gives meaning to the weakness he has described and to his ambition to please Christ. The reference to the judgment seat stops anyone from taking confidence as license.
settings.readers: People raised on Greek ideas of the soul who might hear a hope of escape from the body, and Jewish believers raised on a resurrection hope; the passage speaks to both by joining a hope of being with the Lord and a hope for a new body.
views: Paul is telling of his own expectation after nearly dying.
Paul is giving the church a picture of what happens to every believer at death.

settings.what: The appeal: why Paul persuades, and the message of reconciliation
settings.to: The Corinthians, and through them the world he describes
settings.when: At the end of the first great section of his defense, before the appeal of 6:1–13
settings.why: To say what drives him (the love of Christ and the fear of the Lord), what he preaches (reconciliation), and what he asks ("be reconciled to God"). The paragraph also gives the Corinthians a way to read themselves: they are not to judge by appearance (5:12, 16), and they are to share in the ministry. The appeal of 5:20 is addressed to the church itself, as well as to outsiders, as 6:1–2 shows.
settings.readers: A church that had been at odds with Paul and with one another: the message of reconciliation is first of all a call back to each other.
views: The "you" of 5:20 is the Corinthians, who need to be reconciled to God and to Paul.
The "you" is anyone who hears the apostolic message, as in evangelistic use of the verse.

traditions.q: What happens between death and the resurrection? (5:1–10)
views: At death each soul is judged. The righteous enter heaven at once or, if they need purifying, pass through purgatory, and all await the resurrection of the body at Christ's return (CCC 1021-1022, 1030-1032).

Orthodox teaching does not accept the Latin doctrine of purgatorial fire; Mark of Ephesus argued against it at the Council of Florence. The church prays for the departed, and Orthodox teachers speak of a foretaste of the final state between death and the last judgment.

The Augsburg Confession teaches the resurrection of the dead and eternal life for the godly (article 17); I found nothing in it that defines the state between death and the resurrection. Scholars read Luther's own statements about the dead differently, some as sleep and some as the soul's life with God.

At death the souls of the righteous are made perfect in holiness and received into the highest heavens, while their bodies return to dust until the resurrection; souls neither die nor sleep (Westminster Confession 32.1). Calvin wrote against soul sleep in his Psychopannychia (written 1534, first printed 1542).

The 1689 Confession (chapter 31, paragraph 1) follows Westminster closely: the bodies return to dust, the souls neither die nor sleep, and the souls of the righteous are received into paradise, where the Westminster text has "the highest heavens."
Seventh-day Adventists teach a state of unconsciousness in death, with conditional immortality.

The dead are "conscious of nothing at all" and wait for a resurrection, which is a re-creation by God of the same individual with a new body. The 144,000 are raised as spirit creatures in heaven, and the great majority look for life on earth.

traditions.q: Are Christians judged for their deeds? (5:10)
views: Every person is judged at death and again at the last judgment, according to deeds of faith and love. The saved receive reward, and those who need it are purified first (CCC 1021–1022, 1038–1041).

Faith is bound to bring forth good fruits, and good works are to be done because of God's will (Augsburg Confession 6). Christ will come to judge, giving the godly eternal life (Augsburg Confession 17).

All persons will appear before the tribunal of Christ to give an account and to receive according to what they have done in the body (Westminster Confession 33.1). Believers' good works are accepted in Christ and rewarded though accompanied with weaknesses (16.6).

All persons will appear before the tribunal of Christ to give an account of their thoughts, words and deeds, and to receive according to what they have done in the body, whether good or evil (London Baptist Confession of 1689, chapter 32, paragraph 1).

Christ died for all without exception. "There is not, never has been, and never will be a single human being for whom Christ did not suffer" (CCC 605, quoting the Council of Quiercy, 853). Not all accept the gift.
Athanasius, On the Incarnation, says that the Word took a body of our nature and was worthy to suffer on behalf of all and to be ambassador for all with the Father (chapters 7-8).

The promise of the Gospel is universal and pertains to all men, and Christ has commanded that repentance and remission of sins be preached in his name among all nations (Formula of Concord, Solid Declaration 11).

The Canons of Dort teach that Christ's death is of infinite value and worth, more than sufficient to atone for the sins of the whole world (second head, article 3), yet that its saving effectiveness works itself out in the chosen ones (article 8). Amyraldians, a school within Calvinism, hold a form of hypothetical universalism.
Wesley preached that the grace of God is "free in all, and free for all" (Free Grace, sermon 128, preached at Bristol).

The 1689 confession says that Christ "certainly and effectually" applies the redemption he obtained to all those for whom he obtained it (chapter 8, paragraph 8), so the Particular Baptists tie the saving effect to those the Father gave him.

Christ entrusted the ministry of reconciliation to the apostles, and it passes to bishops and priests in the sacrament of penance. All the faithful share in the church's task of reconciling (CCC 1442, 1461).
Private absolution is kept in the churches (Augsburg Confession 11).
The keys of the kingdom are the preaching of the holy gospel and Christian discipline (Heidelberg Catechism 83-85).

By his obedience unto death Christ made satisfaction for our sins to the Father (CCC 615-616). Anselm's Cur Deus Homo set out the satisfaction view of the atonement, and Aquinas treats the efficiency of Christ's Passion, including satisfaction, in Summa Theologiae III, q.48.
The Eastern Orthodox Church holds the view of the atonement called recapitulation, in which Jesus became what we are so that we could become what he is.

Christ bore the wrath of God against sin and made satisfaction by his death (Heidelberg Catechism 37-40). By his perfect obedience and sacrifice he fully satisfied the justice of his Father for all those whom the Father has given him (Westminster Confession 8.5).
Wesley preached the active and passive righteousness of Christ as never separated (The Lord Our Righteousness).

The 1689 Confession says God justifies by imputing Christ's active obedience to the whole law and his passive obedience in his death, for the believers' whole and sole righteousness (chapter 11, paragraph 1).
The Dordrecht Confession (1632) treats the restoration of man through the promise of the coming Christ (article 3) and the coming of Christ and the purpose for which he came (article 4).
